children.translated_text: Now, the instruction on <s>yoga</s>.
<s>Yoga</s> is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind.
Then the seer abides in his own form.
At other times, there is conformity with the fluctuations.
The fluctuations are fivefold, afflicted and unafflicted.
They are valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep, and memory.
Perception, inference, and authoritative testimony are valid cognitions.
Error is false knowledge, grounded in a form other than the thing itself.
Conceptual construction is based on verbal knowledge and is empty of a real object.
Sleep is a fluctuation resting on the cognition of absence.
Memory is the non-loss of an experienced object.
Its cessation comes through practice and dispassion.
Of these, practice is the effort toward steadiness in that state.
But it has a firm ground when cultivated for a long time, without interruption, and with reverent care.
Dispassion, called mastery, belongs to one who is free from thirst for objects seen or heard about.
The higher form of that is indifference even toward the guṇas, arising from knowledge of puruṣa.
Cognitive samādhi is accompanied by reasoning, reflection, bliss, and the sense of I-am-ness.
The other samādhi, preceded by the practice of the idea of cessation, leaves only latent impressions.
For the bodiless and those dissolved into prakṛti, it is caused by their state of becoming.
For others, it is preceded by faith, energy, memory, samādhi, and insight.
It is near for those whose intensity is keen.
Because intensity may be mild, moderate, or excessive, there is further distinction even from that.
Or it comes through dedication to īśvara.
Īśvara is a special puruṣa, untouched by afflictions, actions, fruits of action, and latent deposits.
In him the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed.
He is also the teacher of the ancients, because he is not delimited by time.
His verbal expression is praṇava.
Its repetition is to be accompanied by contemplation of its meaning.
From that comes the attainment of inward consciousness and also the absence of obstacles.
Illness, apathy, doubt, heedlessness, laziness, lack of restraint, mistaken vision, failure to attain a stage, and instability are distractions of the mind; these are the obstacles.
Pain, dejection, bodily tremor, inhalation, and exhalation accompany distraction.
For the purpose of counteracting that, there is practice of one principle.
Through cultivation of friendliness, compassion, joy, and equanimity toward happiness, suffering, merit, and demerit, the mind becomes clear.
Or by exhalation and retention of the breath.

children.text: viṣayavatī vā pravṛttir utpannā manasaḥ sthitinibandhinī ||
children.translated_text: Or a sense-activity that has arisen in relation to an object becomes a support for steadiness of the mind.
Or there is the sorrowless and luminous one.
Or the mind may take as its object one who is free from passion.
Or it may rest on knowledge arising from dream and sleep.
Or from meditation on whatever is desired.
Its mastery extends from the smallest atom to the greatest magnitude.

children.text: kṣīṇavṛtter abhijātasyeva maṇer grahītṛgrahaṇagrāhyeṣu tatsthatadañjanatā samāpattiḥ ||
children.translated_text: When its fluctuations have diminished, like a clear jewel, its taking on the color of what is present in the knower, the instrument of knowing, and the known is samāpatti.
There, samāpatti mixed with conceptual distinctions of word, object, and knowledge is savitarka.
When memory is purified, the nirvitarka state appears as though empty of its own form and shining only as the object.

children.text: etayaiva savicārā nirvicārā ca sūkṣmaviṣayā vyākhyātā ||
children.translated_text: By this alone, savicāra and nirvicāra samāpatti, whose objects are subtle, have been explained.
And subtle objectivity extends up to the unmanifest.
Those very states are samādhi with seed.
From proficiency in nirvicāra comes clarity of the inner self.
There the insight is truth-bearing.
It has a different object from insight based on scripture and inference, because its object is particular.
The latent impression born from that obstructs other latent impressions.
When even that is brought to cessation, because all has been brought to cessation, there is seedless samādhi.
Austerity, self-study, and dedication to īśvara are kriyāyoga.
It is for cultivating samādhi and for attenuating the afflictions.
Ignorance, I-am-ness, attachment, aversion, and clinging to life are the afflictions.
Ignorance is the field for the subsequent afflictions, whether dormant, attenuated, interrupted, or fully active.
Ignorance is the apprehension of the impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self as permanent, pure, pleasant, and self.
I-am-ness is the apparent identity of the powers of seeing and of the instrument of seeing.
Attachment follows upon pleasure.
Aversion follows upon pain.
Clinging to life, flowing by its own nature and established even in the learned, is of that same kind.
In their subtle form, these are to be abandoned by return to their source.
Their fluctuations are to be abandoned by meditation.
The store of karma, rooted in affliction, is to be experienced in births seen and unseen.
As long as the root exists, its fruition is birth, span of life, and experience.
These have pleasure and pain as their fruits because of merit and demerit as their causes.

children.text: pariṇāmatāpasaṃskāraduḥkhaguṇavṛttirodhāc ca duḥkham eva sarvaṃ vivekinaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For the discriminating person, all is indeed suffering, because of the suffering caused by change, distress, latent impressions, and the opposition of the guṇa-fluctuations.
The suffering that has not yet come is to be abandoned.
The conjunction of the seer and the seen is the cause of what is to be abandoned.
The seen, whose nature is illumination, activity, and stability, consists of the elements and senses and exists for experience and liberation.
The stages of the guṇas are the particular, the non-particular, the merely marked, and the unmarked.
The seer is mere seeing; though pure, he observes cognitions.
The very nature of the seen exists only for his sake.

children.text: kṛtārthaṃ prati naṣṭam apy anaṣṭaṃ tadanyasādhāraṇatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Though destroyed in relation to one whose purpose is fulfilled, it is not destroyed, because it is common to others.
Conjunction is the cause of apprehending the own nature of the powers of the possessed and the possessor.
Its cause is ignorance.
Because of the absence of that, there is absence of conjunction; this is abandonment, the isolation of that seer.
Unwavering discriminative discernment is the means of abandonment.
For that person, insight reaches its final ground in seven ways.
From the practice of the limbs of yoga, when impurity has been destroyed, the light of knowledge extends up to discriminative discernment.
Restraint, observance, posture, breath-control, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and samādhi are the eight limbs.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibate restraint, and non-possessiveness are the restraints.
These, when not limited by class, place, time, or convention, are the great vow, universal in scope.
Purity, contentment, austerity, study of sacred recitation, and devotion to <s>Īśvara</s> are the observances.
When obstructive thoughts arise, cultivation of the opposite is to be practiced.

children.text: vitarkā hiṃsādayaḥ kṛtakāritānumoditā lobhakrodhamohapūrvakā mṛdumadhyādhimātrā duḥkhājñānānantaphalā iti pratipakṣabhāvanam ||
children.translated_text: Obstructive thoughts, such as violence and the rest, whether done, caused to be done, or approved, preceded by greed, anger, or delusion, and mild, moderate, or intense, have endless fruits of suffering and ignorance; thus one should cultivate the opposite.
When one is established in non-violence, hostility is abandoned in one's presence.
When one is established in truthfulness, actions and their fruits come to depend on one.
When one is established in non-stealing, all jewels come near.
When one is established in celibate restraint, vigor is obtained.
When non-possessiveness is firm, there is understanding of the how and why of birth.
From purity come disgust toward one's own body and non-contact with others.
And there arise purity of sattva, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, conquest of the senses, and fitness for vision of the self.
From contentment, unsurpassed happiness is obtained.
Through austerity, from the destruction of impurity, come perfection of the body and senses.
From study of sacred recitation comes communion with the desired deity.
Perfection in samādhi comes from devotion to <s>Īśvara</s>.
Posture is steady and comfortable.
It is attained through relaxation of effort and absorption into the infinite.
From that, one is not struck by the pairs of opposites.
When that exists, breath-control is the interruption of the movement of inhalation and exhalation.

children.text: sa tu bāhyābhyantarastambhavṛttir deśakālasaṃkhyābhiḥ paridṛṣṭo dīrghasūkṣmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: It has the modes of external, internal, and suspended breath; observed with respect to place, time, and number, it becomes long and subtle.
The fourth transcends the sphere of the external and internal.
From that, the covering over illumination is diminished.
And the mind becomes fit for acts of concentration.
Withdrawal of the senses is, as it were, the senses' imitation of the mind's own form when they are disconnected from their own objects.
From that comes supreme mastery over the senses.
Concentration is the binding of the mind to a place.
There, meditation is the one-streamed continuity of the cognition.
That very meditation, when only the object shines forth and it is as though empty of its own form, is samādhi.
The three together are saṃyama.
From mastery of that, the light of insight arises.
It is to be applied to the stages.
The three are inward limbs in relation to the preceding ones.
Yet even that is an outward limb in relation to seedless samādhi.

The suppression-transformation is the mind's connection with the characteristic of suppression, in which the saṃskāras (latent formations) of emergence and suppression are respectively overpowered and manifested.
Its peaceful flow comes from saṃskāra (latent formation).
The samādhi-transformation of the mind is the subsiding and arising of all-objectness and one-pointedness.
The one-pointedness-transformation of the mind is when the past and arisen cognitions are similar.
By this, the transformations of property, mark, and condition in the elements and senses have been explained.
The property-bearer follows properties that are pacified, arisen, or not yet nameable.
Difference in sequence is the cause of difference in transformations.
From saṃyama on the three transformations comes knowledge of the past and future.
Because word, meaning, and cognition are superimposed on one another, there is confusion; from saṃyama on their distinction comes knowledge of the sounds of all beings.
From direct perception of saṃskāras (latent formations) comes knowledge of former births.
From saṃyama on a cognition comes knowledge of another's mind.
But not together with its support, because that has not become the object of that cognition.
From saṃyama on the form of the body, when the power by which it is grasped is suspended and there is no conjunction with the light of the eye, invisibility results.

children.text: sopakramaṃ nirupakramaṃ ca karma tatsaṃyamād aparāntajñānam ariṣṭebhyo vā ||
children.translated_text: Karma is of two kinds, quick to fructify and slow to fructify; from saṃyama on that comes knowledge of the end of life, or else from omens.
In friendliness and the other attitudes, there are strengths.
Among strengths are the strength of an elephant and the like.
By placing the light of activity, there is knowledge of what is subtle, hidden, or remote.
Knowledge of the worlds comes from saṃyama on the sun.
On the moon, there is knowledge of the arrangement of the stars.
On the pole-star, there is knowledge of their motion.
On the navel-wheel, there is knowledge of the arrangement of the body.
On the hollow of the throat, hunger and thirst cease.
On the tortoise-channel, there is steadiness.
On the light in the head, there is vision of perfected beings.
Or, from intuitive illumination, everything is known.
In the heart, there is awareness of the mind.

children.text: sattvapuruṣayor atyantāsaṃkīrṇayoḥ pratyayāviśeṣaḥ bhogaḥ parārthatvāt svārthasaṃyamāt puruṣajñānam ||
children.translated_text: Experience is the non-distinction of cognition between sattva and puruṣa, which are utterly unmixed; because sattva exists for another, from saṃyama on what exists for itself comes knowledge of puruṣa.
From that arise intuitive, auditory, tactile, visual, gustatory, and olfactory knowledges.
They are obstacles in samādhi, but powers in the state of emergence.
From the loosening of the cause of bondage and from awareness of the pathways, there is entry of the mind into another body.
From mastery of udāna, there is non-attachment in water, mud, thorns, and the like, and also upward departure.
From mastery of samāna comes blazing heat.
From saṃyama on the relation between hearing and space comes divine hearing.
From saṃyama on the relation between body and space, and from absorption into the lightness of cotton, comes movement through space.
The externally unimagined activity is the great disembodied state; from that comes destruction of the covering over illumination.
From saṃyama on grossness, own-form, subtlety, inherence, and purposefulness comes mastery over the elements.
From that arise aṇimā and the other powers, bodily perfection, and non-obstruction by their properties.
Beauty of form, grace, strength, and diamond-like firmness are bodily perfection.
From saṃyama on grasping, own-form, I-am-ness, inherence, and purposefulness comes mastery over the senses.
From that come speed like the mind, the state of being without instruments, and mastery over primordial nature.
For one who has only the discernment of the difference between sattva and puruṣa, there is lordship over all states and omniscience.
Through dispassion even toward that, when the seed of defect is destroyed, there is kaivalya.
When there is an invitation from beings in high places, one should not form attachment or pride, because undesirable consequences would arise again.
From <s>saṃyama</s> (integrated concentration) on moments and their sequence comes knowledge born of discrimination.
From that comes discernment of two things that are alike, because their difference is not delimited by class, characteristic, or place.

children.text: tārakaṃ sarvaviṣayaṃ sarvathāviṣayam akramaṃ ceti vivekajaṃ jñānam ||
children.translated_text: Knowledge born of discrimination is called tāraka, salvific: it has all things as its object, has them in every way as its object, and is non-sequential.
When the purity of <s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s> is equal, there is <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation).
The powers arise from birth, herbs, mantra, austerity, or <s>samādhi</s>.
Transformation into another birth or kind comes from the filling-in by <s>prakṛti</s> (nature).

children.text: nimittam aprayojakaṃ prakṛtīnāṃ varaṇabhedas tu tataḥ kṣetrikavat ||
children.translated_text: The instrumental cause does not impel the <s>prakṛtis</s>; rather, it breaks the obstruction, like a farmer with a field.
Created minds arise from mere I-am-ness.
Although their activities differ, one mind is the impeller of many.
Among these, the mind born of meditation is without a store of karma.
The karma of the yogin is neither white nor black; that of others is of three kinds.
From that, only the latent impressions corresponding to the ripening of that karma become manifest.
Even when separated by birth, place, and time, they have immediate continuity, because memory and saṃskāra have one form.
And these latent impressions are beginningless, because the will-to-live is eternal.
Because they are held together by cause, result, support, and object, when these are absent, they too are absent.
The past and the future exist in their own form, because the properties are distinguished by temporal path.
They, whether manifest or subtle, have the guṇas as their nature.
Because transformation is unified, the reality of an object is established.
Although the object is the same, because minds differ, the paths of the two are distinct.
An object is known or unknown because it depends on the mind's being colored by it.
The fluctuations of the mind are always known, because their master, <s>puruṣa</s>, is unchanging.
The mind is not self-illuminating, because it is something seen.
And both cannot be ascertained at the same time.
If it were seen by another mind, there would be an infinite regress of cognition of cognition, and a confusion of memories.
When consciousness, which does not pass over into another, assumes that form, there is awareness of one's own cognition.
The mind, colored by both seer and seen, has all purposes as its scope.
Though variegated by countless latent impressions, it exists for another, because it acts as an aggregate.
For one who sees the distinction, reflection on the state of selfhood ceases.
Then the mind slopes toward discrimination and inclines toward <s>kaivalya</s>.
In the gaps in that, other cognitions arise from saṃskāras.
Their abandonment has been taught as being like that of the afflictions.

children.text: prasaṃkhyāne 'py akusīdasya sarvathā vivekakhyāter dharmameghaḥ samādhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: For one who is not complacent even about highest insight, because discriminative discernment is complete in every way, there is the <s>dharmamegha</s> samādhi.
From that comes the cessation of afflictions and karma.
Then, because knowledge is infinite when all coverings and impurities have been removed, what remains to be known is little.
From that, for the guṇas whose purpose has been fulfilled, the sequence of transformations comes to an end.
Sequence is correlated with moments and is grasped at the far end of transformation.

children.text: puruṣārthaśūnyānāṃ guṇānāṃ pratiprasavaḥ kaivalyaṃ svarūpapratiṣṭhā vā citiśaktir iti ||
children.translated_text: <s>Kaivalya</s> is the return-to-source of the guṇas, now empty of purpose for <s>puruṣa</s>; or it is the power of consciousness established in its own nature.
